texts.title: Notice: Library Opening Hours
texts.passage_text:
The library is open from Monday to Friday, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. It is closed on Saturdays and Sundays.

If you need a book urgently on the weekend, you can read it online on our website.

Do not enter the library without your student card.

questions.question_text: In this text, "closed" means:
options: not open
very busy
far away

questions.question_text: Is the library open on Sundays?
options: Yes, from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m.
No, it is closed.
Only in an emergency.

questions.question_text: What do you need to enter the library?
options: A staff badge
A library book
A student card

questions.question_text: What is this notice mainly about?
options: When the library is open and what students can do outside those hours
The reason the library recently changed its weekend opening hours
The process for renewing or replacing a lost library card

texts.title: Class Reminder
texts.passage_text:
Dear Ms. Alvarez,

This is a reminder about your English class with Mr. Kim on Thursday, August 13, at 6:30 p.m. Please arrive 15 minutes early because you will need to complete a short form.

If you cannot come to this class, please call us at least 24 hours before, so we can give the spot to another student. Remember to bring your notebook and a pen.

Thank you,
Riverside Language School

questions.question_text: In this message, "spot" most nearly means:
options: a small stain or mark on clothing
a place reserved for someone in a class
a short break between activities

questions.question_text: At what time should the student arrive at the school?
According to the message, what should the student do if she cannot come to the class?
options: Call the school at least 24 hours before
Give her spot to another student herself
Bring her notebook and a pen to the next class

questions.question_text: Which sentence means the same as "Please arrive 15 minutes early"?
options: Come to the school 15 minutes after your class.
Come to the school a quarter of an hour before your class.
Arrive at the school whenever is convenient, with no fixed time.

questions.question_text: What is the main purpose of this message?
options: To cancel the student's next scheduled class because of low enrollment
To request payment for a class that already took place
To remind the student about their class and explain what to bring

texts.title: The Importance of Sleep for Learning
texts.passage_text:
Getting enough sleep is essential for learning new skills, including languages. During deep sleep, the brain organizes the information gathered throughout the day and stores it in long-term memory. However, many students underestimate how much rest they need, especially before an exam or an important class. As a result, they may study for hours but remember very little the next day.

Experts recommend at least seven hours of sleep per night for adults, although this can vary depending on age and lifestyle. Interestingly, taking a short nap after studying can also improve memory, as long as it does not replace a full night's sleep.

questions.question_text: "Underestimate" means:
options: to think something is less important or serious than it really is
to spend far more time studying than is actually necessary
to sleep for a much shorter time than your body actually needs

questions.question_text: "As a result, they may study for hours but remember very little" — "as a result" shows:
options: a surprising contrast
a consequence
a supporting example

questions.question_text: According to the text, a short nap can help memory, but only under what condition?
options: if it happens right before an exam
if the person is already an adult
if it does not replace a full night's sleep

questions.question_text: What is this passage mainly about?
options: The connection between sleep and memory
Different study techniques that can help students improve their grades
Why teenagers usually need more sleep than adults

questions.question_text: Which sentence best summarises the text?
options: Sleep matters mainly the night before an exam, not as a regular habit.
Sleep helps store new information, so rest matters as much as studying.
A short nap after studying can fully replace a full night's sleep.

texts.title: The Four-Day Work Week
texts.passage_text:
Over the past few years, a number of companies around the world have experimented with a four-day working week, usually with staff working the same number of hours over four days instead of five, or in some cases working genuinely fewer hours for the same pay. Early trials reported few negative effects on productivity: some companies even found that output stayed the same or improved, a result that may have been due to employees arriving less tired and taking fewer short absences.

It is often argued that these results should be read with some caution. Many of the companies that volunteered for the trials were already flexible, well-managed organisations that were likely to adapt successfully to almost any change in working patterns; a result from this group cannot simply be assumed to apply to a struggling company with rigid processes. There is also a difference between roles that can be reorganised around output — where finishing a task matters more than the exact hours logged — and roles built around continuous coverage, such as retail or healthcare, where someone still has to be there on the fifth day regardless of how efficient anyone becomes.

None of this means the four-day week does not work; it means the trials so far tell us more about which organisations can adopt it easily than about whether it would succeed everywhere.

questions.question_text: "Output" (as in "output stayed the same or improved") most nearly means:
options: how much work actually gets done
how many people are on the payroll
how positive the atmosphere feels at work
how much money is spent running things

questions.question_text: "Coverage" (as in "roles built around continuous coverage") is closest in meaning to:
options: attention from journalists and the news
protection bought through an insurance plan
someone on hand at all times
guidance given to staff who are new

questions.question_text: According to the text, why did some companies see output stay the same or improve during the trials?
options: Staff arrived more rested and took fewer short breaks from work
The company hired temporary workers to cover the missing day
Staff were offered a bonus to make up for the shorter week
Managers began supervising staff more closely than before

questions.question_text: What does the text suggest about the companies that volunteered for these trials?
options: They were struggling financially and hoping for a fast solution
They were mostly well organised beforehand
They were picked at random by a team of researchers
They were obliged by new regulation to take part

questions.question_text: What point is the text making by contrasting roles that can be "reorganised around output" with roles requiring "continuous coverage"?
options: Coverage-based jobs matter less than output-based ones
The new arrangement fits some jobs more easily
Staff in healthcare oppose the four-day week
Retail and healthcare roles cannot be changed at all

questions.question_text: Which sentence best captures the main idea of the text?
options: The evidence shows the four-day week fails in most sectors
Every business should switch to four days without delay
The trials seem promising but mainly show which firms adapt
The four-day week only works when wages are reduced

questions.question_text: What is the writer mainly doing in the second paragraph?
options: Showing that the people running the trials were not honest
Giving reasons to read the results with caution
Insisting that the four-day week should be dropped altogether
Explaining the exact procedure followed in each trial

questions.question_text: Which sentence best paraphrases: "None of this means the four-day week does not work; it means the trials so far tell us more about which organisations can adopt it easily than about whether it would succeed everywhere"?
options: The trials confirm the four-day week suits every type of business
Only companies above a certain size can make this work
No organisation has tested the four-day week properly so far
The trials mainly show who adapts easily, not whether it works

texts.title: Cutting Your Losses
texts.passage_text:
Economists have a blunt phrase for a mistake most of us have made at least once: throwing good money after bad. The sunk cost fallacy describes the pull toward carrying on with something — a project, a renovation, a doomed relationship — simply because so much has already gone into it, not because carrying on is actually the wiser course. Had the idea been drilled into every manager at business school, a good many companies would be in far better shape today; as things stand, it tends to surface only once the losses are already piling up.

Rarely does anyone pause to ask whether the money is recoverable at all. Once it's sunk, it's sunk, and no amount of wishful thinking will claw it back. Yet walking away from a failing venture can feel like an admission of defeat, so people would rather prop it up a little longer than own up to having got it wrong. Cutting your losses, as the saying goes, is a great deal easier said than done.

Boards of directors are no better at spotting the signs. A project that ought to have been written off years earlier is instead handed yet another round of funding, on the grounds that pulling the plug now would waste everything spent so far — which is, of course, precisely the fallacy at work. Only when the losses become too large to explain away does anyone finally read the writing on the wall.

questions.question_text: The idiom "throwing good money after bad" is closest in meaning to:
options: spending carelessly on things nobody really needed
putting more money into something that is already failing
lending money to people known for not repaying debts
giving money to a cause without checking how it's used

questions.question_text: In "no amount of wishful thinking will claw it back," "claw back" is closest in meaning to:
options: increase the value of something over time
hide something so nobody notices it is missing
exchange one loss for a completely different one
recover something slowly and with difficulty

questions.question_text: What does the sentence "Had the idea been drilled into every manager at business school, a good many companies would be in far better shape today" suggest?
options: Many companies are worse off today because this idea went largely untaught
Business schools currently teach this idea to every manager
Most managers ignored this idea when they were taught it in school
Companies that studied this idea in the past have since forgotten it

questions.question_text: The opening of paragraph 2, "Rarely does anyone pause to ask whether the money is recoverable at all," implies that:
options: People frequently double-check whether their money can be recovered
Recovering the money is usually simple once someone looks into it
Very few people ever ask if the money can be saved
Nobody has ever managed to recover money lost this way

questions.question_text: In the text, choosing to "prop it up a little longer" rather than "own up to having got it wrong" means a person would rather:
options: sell the project quickly than wait for it to improve
keep a failing project going than admit their mistake
blame someone else than accept responsibility publicly
ask a colleague for help than solve the problem alone

questions.question_text: The comment that cutting your losses "is a great deal easier said than done" suggests that:
options: very few people actually understand what this phrase means
experts disagree about whether this is good financial advice
this approach works well only for very small amounts of money
doing this is much harder than simply talking about it

questions.question_text: Which sentence best captures the main idea of the text?
options: People keep funding failure because stopping feels worse than losing more
Most organisations recover their losses eventually if they wait long enough
Boards of directors are less rational than individual investors
Financial mistakes are usually caused by a lack of proper training

questions.question_text: What is the writer mainly doing in the final paragraph?
options: Proving that boards of directors are dishonest with shareholders
Recommending a new method for approving company funding
Showing that the same pattern happens in organisations too
Arguing that projects should never be given a second round of funding

questions.question_text: Which statement best paraphrases "which is, of course, precisely the fallacy at work"?
options: This decision is completely different from the fallacy described earlier
This is a clear case of the very mistake just described
The fallacy only applies to individuals, never to a whole board
Nobody has ever proven that this decision is actually a mistake

questions.question_text: What does it mean for a board to finally "read the writing on the wall"?
options: They publish a public report explaining what went wrong
They discover a written warning that had been hidden from them
They decide to write off the entire company as a loss
They finally accept an outcome they can no longer avoid
